claims.claim: Across the 34 surveyed CRM/agentic systems, zero reach continuity-A: deterministic replay of a decision from an immutable event plane. The best in field is grade B (genuine timelines/audit logs on mutable current-state storage).
claims.counterevidence: Falsifier F1: any one surveyed vendor demonstrating deterministic replay of a decision from an immutable event plane kills this claim; republish the scoreboard. Falsifier F3: a production CRM shipping continuity-A kills outright. Falsifier F4: a CRM rebuilding its core state machine on an event-sourced core the way Temporal rebuilds workflows kills the claim. Falsifier F2 (dependency, unresolved here): the 99h convergence lane's Attio/Clay/Apollo/HubSpot archaeology may surface event-sourced internals in an in-category system; internals-only narrows the claim, shipped product behavior kills it. Conjunction caveat (L6 review): the definition's two conjuncts are individually occupied elsewhere (Temporal for replay, immudb for tamper-evidence); the claim is that no surveyed in-category system combines both, and the demand for the combined standard is unobserved (the survey does not establish market size that would pay for continuity-A).
claims.independent_support: Per-claim evidence grades documented in the survey report; the survey itself is documented primary research; this session's re-verification (CLS2-04 through CLS2-06) independently confirmed the grade-B inventory.
claims.maximum_defensible_wording: As of 2026-09-30, across the 34 CRM/agentic systems surveyed, zero systems meet the continuity-A definition (deterministic replay of a decision from an immutable event plane). The claim is survey-bounded, not universal; grades are the survey's own, bounded by vendor-described claims where independence was unavailable.
claims.primary_source: research_notes/crm-agentic-harvest-20260930/report.md section 5 scoreboard and sections 2-4 per-system continuity reasoning
claims.public_wording: We surveyed 34 CRM and agentic systems for one behavior: can they replay a past decision deterministically from an immutable event plane? Zero could. Everyone ships audit logging; nobody ships replay.
claims.scope: 34 systems surveyed 2026-09-30 (modern CRMs, agentic sales, agentic marketing, business OSes); does not establish market size that would pay for continuity-A

claims.claim: Temporal proves deterministic replay is engineerable in workflow infrastructure: Event History is the complete ordered log of everything that happened in a workflow; workers re-run workflow code against recorded events instead of restoring snapshots; non-determinism is policed mechanically (Date.now(), Math.random(), direct network calls banned; replay-safe APIs return recorded values); the WorkflowReplayer replays a workflow against a recorded history to verify code changes stay deterministic.
claims.counterevidence: Falsifier F4 (kills the C1 slot, not this precedent): a CRM rebuilding its core state machine on an event-sourced core the way Temporal rebuilds workflows. The objection that Temporal's domain is workflow orchestration, not CRM/agent decisions, bounds scope rather than refuting the precedent. Retention limits and absent tamper-evidence bound what the replay plane can promise. The narrowed two-layer standard of C1 is literally Temporal's documented agent architecture (LLM calls as Activities, recorded results returned during replay), which reduces the novelty to category non-adoption, not a missing primitive.
claims.independent_support: None independent this session. Temporal's own documentation plus the open-source Swift SDK (the source is the vendor's own repo/docs).
claims.maximum_defensible_wording: Per Temporal's own documentation, Event History provides replay of workflow execution: workers re-run code against recorded events and non-determinism is policed mechanically. This is the closest existing engineering to the thesis's standard, in the workflow-infrastructure domain. It is not independently tested here; histories have retention limits and no cryptographic tamper-evidence. It shows the primitive is described and shipped in another domain; it does not show CRM/agent adoption.
claims.primary_source: docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/event-history; apple/swift-temporal-sdk WorkflowReplayer documentation
claims.public_wording: Deterministic replay already exists in workflow infrastructure. Temporal workers do not restore snapshots; they re-run code against recorded events. The primitive is real. The CRM category has simply not adopted it.
claims.scope: workflow orchestration only; supports the thesis that the standard is engineerable, not that it is adopted in CRM/agentic systems Bounds verified by the L6 review: Temporal histories have retention limits and carry no cryptographic tamper-evidence.

claims.claim: The operative standard is defined as: deterministic derivations (scores, projections, transitions) replayable from a pinned immutable event plane. Bit-identical replay of LLM-agent generation is explicitly excluded as the wrong standard. Agent generation itself gets the Fin-grade honest standard: replay-the-artifact as proof of fix.
claims.counterevidence: The L6 steelman (bit-identical replay is a strawman for agentic systems) reshaped this definition; it is recorded as the narrowing that produced this wording, not as a refutation. If deterministic generation replay ever becomes the relevant buyer demand, this definition would need revision.
claims.independent_support: The definition is our own methodological commitment, adopted after the adversarial review in DEEP-RESEARCH-C1-REPLAYABLE-EVIDENCE.md section 5.
claims.maximum_defensible_wording: The standard C1 argues for is deterministic derivations (scores, projections, transitions) replayable from a pinned immutable event plane. It does not require bit-identical replay of LLM-agent generation; that reading is explicitly disclaimed.
claims.primary_source: DEEP-RESEARCH-C1-REPLAYABLE-EVIDENCE.md section 3 (the narrowed claim) and section 5 (adversarial answer)
claims.public_wording: We are not asking for bit-identical replay of an AI's generation. The standard is narrower: deterministic derivations, scores, projections, transitions, replayable from a pinned immutable event plane. The replay question is about the deterministic layer around the agent, not the agent's own output.
claims.scope: the C1 piece's own product standard; does not bind any vendor

claims.claim: Asana's task stories are lossy: the web app consolidates multiple changes by one user to one data element within a 24-hour period into only the last change, and the API returns only the same stream as the web app (the API team has no separate story stream).
claims.counterevidence: None this session. If Asana ships an immutable event stream distinct from the web-app story stream, regrade.
claims.independent_support: Corroborated by two additional Asana forum threads (41521, 22045); Phil Seeman is a recognized Asana API community authority.
claims.maximum_defensible_wording: Per Phil Seeman's canonical forum explanation, the Asana web app performs story 'consolidation': multiple changes by one user to a data element within 24 hours, with no other users changing it in between, get consolidated so only the last change is reported; the API team has no separate story stream, so the API returns only what the web app shows. The B (lossy) grade stands, independently sourced.
claims.primary_source: forum.asana.com/t/is-there-a-truthful-audit-trail/55127 (Phil Seeman canonical explanation)
claims.public_wording: Asana's activity stories are lossy. Multiple changes to the same field within a day get consolidated into the last one, and the API sees only the same consolidated stream as the web app.
claims.scope: Asana task stories; consolidation behavior as described on the forum

claims.claim: Martin Fowler's established guidance on event sourcing: capture all changes as a sequence of events; rebuild state by re-running the log; audit trail and reconstruction 'come for free'. The pattern's costs are equally established: eventual consistency, event schema evolution (history is never rewritten, so old events must stay readable forever), and more moving parts. Apply it where the benefits justify the cost, not as a blanket mandate.
claims.counterevidence: None. The cost argument belongs in the standard's own documentation, not as a refutation; it is the reason the unoccupied slot is a genuine differentiator rather than a free lunch.
claims.independent_support: Long-standing primary source; cited as common knowledge attributed to its author.
claims.maximum_defensible_wording: Fowler's formulation of event sourcing (capture changes as an event sequence, rebuild state by re-running the log, audit trail comes free) and its costs (eventual consistency, permanent schema evolution burden, more moving parts) are established. His guidance: apply where benefits justify the cost. The cost caveat is real and is part of the standard, not a refutation of it.
claims.primary_source: martinfowler.com/eaaDev/EventSourcing.html
claims.public_wording: Event sourcing is textbook architecture, not a new invention, and its costs are textbook too: eventual consistency, event schemas you must read forever, more moving parts. The honest version of the standard carries the cost caveat with it.
claims.scope: Fowler's published guidance; the costs frame any immutability/replay standard honestly

claims.claim: GDPR Article 17 erasure versus append-only history is a direct legal contradiction; the accepted reconciliation is crypto-shredding (per-subject data-encryption keys, key destroyed on erasure), treated as a pragmatic near-equivalent to erasure in EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 (adopted 2026-04-08). Immutability carries a real legal engineering cost, which is one reason CRMs avoid it.
claims.counterevidence: None this session. The contradiction is acknowledged in the thesis's own design; crypto-shredding is engineerable but unshipped in the surveyed category.
claims.independent_support: Third-party engineering writeups (handbook-academy engineering handbook, fractonicmind/ternarylogic) plus adversarial review in trilamsr/regatta#548.
claims.maximum_defensible_wording: GDPR Article 17 erasure directly contradicts append-only history. The accepted reconciliation is crypto-shredding: per-subject data-encryption keys, key destroyed on erasure, treated as a pragmatic near-equivalent to erasure in EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 adopted 2026-04-08. Immutability therefore carries a real legal engineering cost, one reason CRMs avoid it.
claims.primary_source: GDPR Article 17; EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 (adopted 2026-04-08); handbook-academy engineering handbook; fractonicmind/ternarylogic; trilamsr/regatta#548
claims.public_wording: Append-only history collides directly with GDPR erasure law. The accepted engineering answer is crypto-shredding: encrypt per subject, destroy the key on erasure. It is real, it costs engineering effort, and it is one more reason the category avoids immutability.
claims.scope: the legal-engineering tension only; does not claim any surveyed vendor ships crypto-shredding

claims.maximum_defensible_wording: The survey's convergence pattern: every surveyed system ships audit logging (answers 'what changed'); none ships deterministic replay (answers 'can you prove this decision would be made again, identically, from the same evidence').
